what_it_does: Robots that navigate complex environments often use a two-step approach: a neural network guesses which direction to go, and then a classical planning algorithm (called Model Predictive Control, or MPC) refines that guess by simulating many possible futures and picking the best path. These two steps have very different computational shapes — the neural network wants to crunch many numbers in parallel, while MPC involves irregular, unpredictable calculations that change moment to moment — and ordinary chips handle this mix poorly. HiPER is a custom chip (a purpose-built integrated circuit, or ASIC) with 1024 small processing units arranged in a nested, tree-like communication structure that lets different parts of the chip naturally shift between the dense and the sparse phases of this workload. A six-level scheduling system manages what each unit does at each moment without needing a complex central controller, allowing the chip to adapt fluidly as the robot's computation switches between neural-network mode and planning mode.
